questions.question: Why does Susanoo go to Takamagahara (the High Plain of Heaven) to visit Amaterasu before his exile?
options: A. To challenge Amaterasu for control of the heavenly realm
B. To say farewell before departing for Yomi to be with his dead mother
C. To deliver the sword Kusanagi as a tribute
D. To confess responsibility for the destruction of the rice paddies
questions.explanation: Susanoo has been weeping and refusing his assigned realm because he wants to go to Yomi to be with his dead mother Izanami. Izanagi exiles him for this, and before departing Susanoo goes to say farewell to Amaterasu. His arrival triggers Amaterasu's suspicion, leading to the contest and then the rampage.

questions.question: How do the eight million gods succeed in luring Amaterasu out of the Ama-no-Iwato?
options: A. They threaten to seal the cave permanently and choose a new sun goddess
B. They create a spectacle of laughter and revelry; when Amaterasu cracks the door to investigate, she sees her own reflection and is transfixed
C. The god Ame-no-Tajikarao breaks down the door with his great strength
D. Susanoo apologizes from outside the cave, and Amaterasu forgives him and emerges
questions.explanation: The strategy is to make Amaterasu curious — to create a scene so joyous and incomprehensible that she must look. Ame-no-Uzume's dance makes the gods laugh; Amaterasu hears this and cracks the door. She then sees her own reflection in the Yata no Kagami mirror and is transfixed long enough for Ame-no-Tajikarao to pull her fully out.

questions.question: The Yata no Kagami (sacred mirror) produced during the Ama-no-Iwato episode became one of the three imperial regalia of Japan.
questions.explanation: The mirror forged and hung outside the cave to lure Amaterasu out becomes, along with the sword Kusanagi (found by Susanoo in Yamata no Orochi) and the Magatama beads (also present at the cave), one of Japan's three imperial regalia — the physical symbols of legitimate imperial authority transmitted through the divine lineage.

questions.question: Susanoo is responsible for the disaster that caused Amaterasu to hide, and he is eventually punished and exiled. But the Kojiki also shows him as a hero who saves a young woman and discovers a sacred sword. What does this tell you about how the Kojiki treats its divine figures?
questions.sample_answer: The Kojiki does not present its gods as simple moral agents who are either wholly good or wholly bad. Susanoo is genuinely destructive and genuinely heroic. His violence causes cosmic crisis; his courage and cleverness later produce the sword that becomes an imperial relic. This moral complexity is characteristic of the text's divine figures — they are powerful forces with distinct natures, not moral exemplars. Reading them as simple heroes or villains misses the text's actual structure.
key_concepts: storm as both destructive and generative
same deity in different narrative registers

questions.question: The sword Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi becomes an imperial relic after being discovered by Susanoo. Where does he find it?
options: A. In the treasury of the sea god's palace
B. Hidden in the rock cave beside Amaterasu's chamber
C. Inside the tail of the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi, after slaying it
D. Buried under the pillar that Izanagi and Izanami erected on Onogoro Island
questions.explanation: After intoxicating the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi with sake and slaying it, Susanoo finds the sword Kusanagi inside one of its tails. He presents it to Amaterasu. This sword — along with the mirror and jewels from the Ama-no-Iwato episode — becomes one of Japan's three imperial regalia.
